slides.head:
Six carriers vanished
for eleven days.
slides.body: Washington knew war was coming. It looked everywhere but Hawaii.
slides.date: SWIPE FOR THE FOUR DAYS THAT SET IT IN MOTION
26 NOV 1941 · 6 A.M. TOKYO TIME · HITOKAPPU BAY
slides.head: The fleet weighs anchor.
slides.body: Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu, Shokaku and Zuikaku, carrying more than 400 aircraft, steam east into an ocean almost no ship crosses.

slides.date: THE ROUTE · DATES IN TOKYO TIME
slides.head: Chosen for its emptiness.
slides.body: The late autumn North Pacific is cold, rough and nearly free of shipping. The fleet keeps total radio silence the whole way.

slides.quote: I have washed my hands of it, and it is now in the hands of you and Knox, the Army and the Navy.
slides.who: Secretary of State Cordell Hull to Secretary of War Henry Stimson, the morning after the Hull note

slides.head: “This despatch is to be considered a war warning.”
slides.body: Admiral Harold Stark warns the Pacific Fleet that an aggressive move by Japan is expected within days.

slides.head: Hawaii is not on the list.
slides.body: The warning names the Philippines, Thailand's Kra Peninsula and Borneo. Japan's invasion forces really are gathering there.

slides.head: One carrier is already at war.
slides.body: Enterprise sails to fly Marine Wildcats to Wake Island. Battle Order No. 1: “Steady nerves and stout hearts are needed now.”

slides.head: The last chance to speak.
slides.body: Eight former prime ministers meet before the Emperor. Most doubt Japan can win a long war. None says plainly that war is wrong.

slides.head: No one in the room knows.
slides.body: The carriers are already three days out, somewhere in the fog. They can still be called back if the talks succeed.

slides.head: Climb Mount Niitaka
slides.body: Tokyo makes its final decision, and one coded signal sends the fleet the rest of the way.
slides.cta: Follow so you don't miss it
